The quiet morning opens with light, dust, and soft breathing.
I remember paper maps folded into gloves, warm dashboard sun.
Somewhere a kettle sings, and the kitchen remembers being small.
Rain taps the window like patient fingers asking to enter.
The old dog lifts his head, listens, then sighs down.
A clock ticks, gathering moments into a small wooden body.
I think of roads I never took, still glowing faintly.
There is a blue cup waiting on the counter today.
Steam rises, curling mistakes into something that almost looks noble.
Outside, a neighbor laughs, and the hedge grows greener somehow.
Words arrive like birds, landing where they please, not mine.
I offer crumbs, silence, and a chair beside the window.
They peck at hours until afternoon bends into gold again.
Somewhere a child learns a new word and drops it.
The word becomes a coin under the couch, forgotten, bright.
I want to write something honest, but honesty wears coats.
It hides in pockets, keys, receipts, and other small delays.
The door opens and closes, carrying weather from another life.
I count my breaths and lose the count, which helps.
Even the calendar forgets its own importance when left alone.
A pencil rolls away, choosing darkness underneath the heavy book.
The book contains answers, but the margins hold better questions.
I miss people I have not met, future versions perhaps.
They wave from trains, carrying luggage full of unread letters.
Night comes early sometimes, wearing a coat of thin clouds.
The streetlamp wakes before the stars and claims its corner.
A cat crosses the yard, intent on invisible urgent business.
I should water plants, yet I keep watering my thoughts.
Thoughts grow wild, mint and thorn, spilling over the edges.
The kettle returns to its song, louder this time, insistent.
I pour tea into the blue cup and watch steam.
Steam writes a sentence, then erases itself without any apology.
Maybe that is wisdom, appearing fully and then letting go.
My hands remember cold winters and the warmth of pockets.
Pockets hold useless treasures: string, buttons, one smooth green stone.
The stone once lived near a river, loved by currents.
I imagine rivers as long sentences, crossing continents, seeking breathing.
Breathing is the first poem, repeated until the world answers.
Answers arrive as rain, as soup, as someone saying yes.
Sometimes no is a fence, keeping the garden intact somehow.
The fence has gaps where small animals carry seeds through.
Seeds do not ask permission; they lean toward whatever shines.
I lean toward the window, where evening arranges its colors.
Colors fade into blue, then black, then memory, then sleep.
Sleep is a country with no maps, only returning dreams.
In dreams, my grandmother hums while folding endless white sheets.
The sheets smell like sunlight and soap, impossible to keep.
I wake with the smell gone and a strange peace.
Peace can be quiet, but it can also be soup.
I heat soup, listening to the spoon tap against porcelain.
Porcelain holds small landscapes, blue rivers painted under clear glaze.
I drink from those rivers and feel faintly like time.
Time is a generous thief, returning things disguised as lessons.
Lessons hide inside chores, waiting for hands to understand them.
Washing dishes becomes prayer when bubbles hold the ceiling light.
Light fills the sink, and I rescue a falling spoon.
The spoon reflects my face, curved and amused, slightly distorted.
Distortion is honest, maybe, because seeing requires some bending always.
Always is a long word, longer than rivers, almost patient.
Patient things gather dust, yet dust is just slow light.
Slow light lands on shelves, books, plants, and forgotten cups.
I wipe it away, then watch it return, not offended.
Offense is heavy luggage, and I have limited storage space.
Space opens when I forgive, or when I forget names.
Names are sweet hooks; they pull a person into presence.
Presence is sitting with soup while steam explains the evening.
Evening asks nothing, except perhaps a lamp and one breath.
Breath enters, leaves, and between those travels there is room.
Room enough for regret, rocks, laughter, and the blue cup.
The cup has a chip shaped like a tiny mountain.
Mountain chips remind me that broken edges can still hold.
Holding is work: cups, memories, promises, warm hands, cold nights.
Nights need lanterns, even if lanterns are only small words.
Words can be lanterns when placed near someone standing alone.
Alone is not always empty; sometimes it is a bell.
A bell rings without asking whether anyone is listening closely.
Closeness grows slowly, like moss on stone, like shared tea.
Tea steeps and darkens, turning water into a gentle story.
Stories need listeners, even if listeners are only kitchen chairs.
Chairs creak when they remember people, weight, laughter, and arguments.
Arguments leave scuff marks on floors that refuse explanations afterward.
Afterward, we sweep, and sweeping becomes another kind of talking.
Talking to oneself is not lonely if replies are kind.
Kindness can be a sandwich cut into careful triangles today.
Triangles hold peanut butter, time, and the memory of lunchboxes.
Lunchboxes rattle down hallways, small planets with handles and secrets.
Secrets ripen, fall, and sometimes sprout into surprising new friendships.
Friendships are weather, changing, returning, leaving umbrellas by the door.
The door knows everyone by the sound of arriving home.
Home is less a place than a repeated warm gesture.
Gesture becomes rhythm: keys, kettle, footsteps, and the opening page.
Page turns like a wing, revealing what was folded away.
Away is not gone; it waits behind ordinary pauses nearby.
Pauses stitch sentences, hearts, rooms, and weather into continuity together.
Together we eat, speak, forget, remember, and clean the table.
Table crumbs are tiny archives of meals and conversations held.
Held words soften, even when they carry sharp edges originally.
Originally, I planned nothing, and nothing planned me back gently.
Gently, the blue cup waits, full, warm, and enough now.
Enough is a thousand small words breathing beside each other.
